title: Memorize one
hookLine: the tradition of carrying hadith by heart: why al-Nawawi cut the chains from his forty
tomorrow: one hadith, by heart. now: who gets to pass it on?

lines: THE CHAIN: WHO HEARD IT FROM WHOM.
cards: Every one of the forty-two is a search away. Type two words and the whole hadith appears, with the chain of who heard it from whom. So here's an odd detail in al-Nawawi's introduction.
The chain is the thing hadith scholars check most carefully; a report stands or falls on it. And al-Nawawi says he left the chains out. On purpose.
Why would a careful scholar cut the very part his field is built to check?

teach.h: SO THEY'D BE EASY TO MEMORIZE.
teach.b: He tells us why: so they'd be easier to memorize. He wasn't writing for a shelf. He was writing for a head.

The chains still sit in the big collections, and he names the collection after each hadith, so anyone can check. But the version he handed on was light enough to carry. That's an old habit in this tradition.

The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, said, in a report Abu Dawud and Tirmidhi record, in paraphrase: may Allah brighten the face of someone who hears a saying from us, keeps it in memory, and passes it on as he heard it.
Then a twist: perhaps the one who carries knowledge carries it to someone who understands it better than he does.

teach.h: THE CARRIER NEEDN'T BE THE EXPERT.
teach.b: So the one who memorizes doesn't have to be the expert. The job is to keep it whole and hand it over. A phone keeps the words.
Memory keeps them with you: in the car, in a hard conversation, at two in the morning with no signal and nobody to ask.
The Arabic for memorizing is hifz, and a hafiz is someone who holds the whole Qur'an by heart.
One hadith is a much smaller start. Something to tell a friend tonight: al-Nawawi trimmed his forty so they'd fit in a memory.

how: Muslim children and adults often memorize hadith alongside the Qur'an, repeating a short report aloud until it comes without looking; al-Nawawi's forty is a common first collection to learn by heart.

games.q: your cousin wants to memorize hadith but says, 'what's the point? I don't understand the commentaries yet.' what does today's hadith say?
o: wait until you understand it fully; memorizing without that is empty.
keep it whole and pass it on; someone may understand it better than you.
skip the words; the commentaries matter more than the hadith itself.
games.why: the hadith blesses the one who keeps a saying and passes it on as heard, and says the next person may understand it better.

practice: Pick one of the forty, the shortest one you like: don't be angry, or actions are by intentions. Say it out loud three times, then cover it and say it once without looking.
For the sit, keep repeating it softly, until it comes without reaching.

wordCard.voice: Memorize one: carry a single hadith by heart, whole and as you heard it, so it goes wherever you go.

orig.note: Arabic: memorizing, keeping safe. a hafiz is someone who holds the whole Qur'an by heart.

carryVoice: For the road: one, by heart, the part a phone can't do for you. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: al-Nawawi, al-Arba'in al-Nawawiyyah, introduction (he gives them without their chains so they are easier to memorize, and names each one's collection)
